topics.name: Basic economic ideas and resource allocation

questions.q: A positive statement is one that…
questions.why: Normative statements contain opinions about what ought to be.

questions.q: The ceteris paribus assumption means…
questions.why: It isolates the effect of one variable.

questions.q: In a mixed economy, resources are allocated by…
o: both the market and the state
questions.why: Most economies combine private markets with public provision.

questions.q: An economy has unemployed workers. How is this shown on a production possibility curve?
o: A shift of the PPC to the left
A shift of the PPC to the right
questions.why: Examiners (2023): the most common error was shifting the PPC left rather than showing a point inside the curve.

questions.q: An economy on its production possibility curve moves from 60 cars and 40 tractors to 50 cars and 60 tractors. What is the opportunity cost of each extra tractor?
questions.why: 10 cars are given up to gain 20 tractors, so each extra tractor costs 10 ÷ 20 = 0.5 cars.

long.q: Use a production possibility curve to explain the meaning of opportunity cost.
scheme: B1: opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up
B1: a PPC shows the combinations of two goods that can be made with all resources fully used
B1: moving along the curve, making more of one good means making less of the other: that amount is the opportunity cost

topics.name: The price system and the microeconomy

questions.q: Income elasticity of demand is negative. The good is…
questions.why: Demand for inferior goods falls as income rises.

questions.q: Cross elasticity of demand between two goods is positive. They are…
questions.why: A rise in one's price raises demand for the other.

questions.q: Consumer surplus is…
o: the difference between what consumers are willing to pay and what they pay
questions.why: It is the area below the demand curve and above the price.

questions.q: If demand is price inelastic, a price rise will…
questions.why: Quantity falls proportionally less than price rises.

questions.q: Incomes rise by 5% and the quantity demanded of a good rises by 10%. What is its income elasticity of demand and what type of good is it?
o: +2, a normal good that is income elastic
questions.why: YED = +10% ÷ +5% = +2; a positive value shows a normal good, and a value above 1 means demand is income elastic.

long.q: When the price of a good rises from $10 to $12, the quantity demanded falls from 500 to 450 units. Calculate the price elasticity of demand and explain what happens to total revenue.
scheme: M1: % change in quantity = −10%; % change in price = +20%
B1: demand is price inelastic
B1: total revenue rises, from $5000 to $5400

questions.q: An indirect tax on a good with inelastic demand falls mainly on…
questions.why: Producers can pass most of the tax on as higher prices.

questions.q: A negative externality of production leads a free market to…
questions.why: Firms ignore external costs, so marginal social cost exceeds private cost.

questions.q: A public good is…
questions.why: These features create the free-rider problem.

questions.q: A specific tax of $4 per unit is imposed and the market price rises from $10 to $13. How is the burden of the tax shared?
o: Consumers $3 per unit, producers $1 per unit
Consumers $1 per unit, producers $3 per unit
Consumers $2 per unit, producers $2 per unit
questions.why: Consumers pay $3 more per unit; producers receive $13 − $4 = $9, which is $1 less than before.

questions.q: A government sets a minimum price for wheat above the equilibrium price. What is the most likely result?
o: A shortage and a black market
A surplus that the government may have to buy up
questions.why: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, so there is excess supply that must be stored, bought or destroyed.

long.q: Explain why a maximum price set below the equilibrium price may lead to a shortage and a black market.
scheme: B1: at the lower price quantity demanded rises
B1: and quantity supplied falls
B1: so there is excess demand (a shortage)
B1: some buyers will pay more than the legal price, so goods are sold illegally above it

questions.q: Aggregate demand is…
questions.why: Consumption, investment, government spending and net exports.

questions.q: Cost-push inflation is caused by…
o: rising costs of production, such as wages or oil
questions.why: Higher costs shift short-run aggregate supply left.

questions.q: Which is counted as unemployed?
o: Someone able and willing to work and actively seeking work
questions.why: The ILO definition requires being without work, available and looking.

questions.q: On an AD/AS diagram, what should the axes be labelled?
o: Price level and real output (real GDP)
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many labelled the axes 'price' and 'quantity' and the curves 'D' and 'S' instead of AD and AS.

questions.q: Demand-pull inflation is best explained as:
o: A rise in costs of production
A fall in the money supply
An increase in AD not matched by spare capacity in AS
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many did not refer to AD, or did not say the AD rise is not matched by spare capacity.

long.q: Distinguish between demand-pull and cost-push inflation.
scheme: B1: demand-pull: aggregate demand rises faster than aggregate supply / the economy's capacity
B1: an example cause: rising consumer spending, lower interest rates, more government spending
B1: cost-push: rising costs of production push up the price level (AS shifts left)
B1: an example cause: higher wages, oil or import prices, a weaker exchange rate

questions.q: Expansionary fiscal policy involves…
o: raising government spending or cutting taxes
questions.why: It boosts aggregate demand.

questions.q: Supply-side policies aim to…
o: increase the productive capacity of the economy
questions.why: Examples: education, training, deregulation, infrastructure.

questions.q: Which is an example of expansionary fiscal policy?
questions.why: Fiscal policy uses tax and spending; monetary policy uses interest rates and money supply.

questions.q: Which policy aims to reduce a current account deficit through expenditure-switching rather than expenditure-reducing?
questions.why: Tariffs make imports dearer, switching spending towards domestic goods; the other policies reduce total spending, including on imports.

questions.q: Which is an example of a conflict between macroeconomic objectives?
o: Cutting income tax may raise both employment and growth
Supply-side policies may lower inflation and unemployment together
Cutting interest rates to reduce unemployment may raise inflation
Higher productivity may improve both growth and the current account
questions.why: Lower interest rates raise aggregate demand, which reduces unemployment but can push up the price level, so one objective is traded off against another.

long.q: Explain how a rise in the central bank's rate of interest might reduce inflation.
scheme: B1: borrowing becomes more expensive and saving more rewarding
B1: so consumption and investment fall
B1: aggregate demand falls (also via a stronger exchange rate cutting net exports)
B1: so demand-pull pressure on the price level eases

questions.q: Comparative advantage means a country should specialise where it has…
questions.why: Trade can benefit both countries even if one is better at everything.

questions.q: The Marshall–Lerner condition states a depreciation improves the current account if…
questions.why: Sum of export and import price elasticities (absolute values) must exceed 1.

questions.q: On a diagram of a currency market, the vertical axis is:
o: The exchange rate (price of the currency)
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many labelled the vertical axis 'price' rather than the price of the currency or exchange rate.

questions.q: Where are remittances from workers abroad recorded in the balance of payments?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): 39% chose the wrong option; remittances are current transfers, recorded in secondary income.

questions.q: A country's export price index rises from 100 to 110 while its import price index rises from 100 to 125. What is its terms of trade index?
questions.why: Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100 = 110 ÷ 125 × 100 = 88, a deterioration.

long.q: A worker in Country A can make 10 units of wheat or 5 units of cloth. A worker in Country B can make 6 units of wheat or 6 units of cloth. Explain which country has a comparative advantage in each good.
scheme: M1: opportunity cost of 1 cloth: A gives up 2 wheat, B gives up 1 wheat
M1: opportunity cost of 1 wheat: A gives up 0.5 cloth, B gives up 1 cloth
B1: A has the comparative advantage in wheat
B1: B has the comparative advantage in cloth, so each should specialise and trade

topics.name: The price system and the microeconomy (A Level)

questions.q: A firm maximises profit where…
questions.why: Producing one more unit would add more to cost than to revenue beyond that point.

questions.q: In perfect competition in the long run, firms earn…
questions.why: Free entry and exit remove supernormal profit.

questions.q: A natural monopoly arises because of…
o: economies of scale so large that one firm has the lowest cost
questions.why: Examples include water and electricity grids.

questions.q: At its profit-maximising output, a perfectly competitive firm faces a price of $10, average cost of $12 and average variable cost of $9. What should it do in the short run?
o: Shut down immediately, because it makes a loss
Keep producing, because price covers average variable cost
Increase output until price equals average cost
questions.why: Price above AVC means each unit adds something towards fixed costs, so the loss is smaller than shutting down; a price-taker cannot raise its price.

questions.q: In the kinked demand curve model of oligopoly, prices tend to be stable because…
o: rivals follow a price rise but ignore a price cut
firms always collude openly to fix prices
rivals match a price cut but ignore a price rise
questions.why: A price rise loses customers to rivals who keep prices down, while a cut is matched and gains little, so firms have no incentive to change price.

long.q: Explain why a profit-maximising monopolist produces where marginal cost equals marginal revenue, and why this may be allocatively inefficient.
scheme: B1: below MC = MR, extra units add more to revenue than cost
B1: beyond it, extra units add more to cost than revenue
B1: allocative efficiency needs P = MC
B1: the monopolist's price is above MC, so output is restricted

questions.q: The Gini coefficient measures…
questions.why: 0 means perfect equality; 1 means maximum inequality.

questions.q: Government failure occurs when…
o: intervention leads to a less efficient allocation of resources
questions.why: Causes include poor information and unintended consequences.

questions.q: Why might a government provide education even though it is excludable?
o: It is a merit good with positive externalities that would be under-consumed
questions.why: Examiners (2023): link merit goods, positive externalities and allocative efficiency.

questions.q: A national minimum wage is set above the equilibrium wage in a competitive labour market. What is the most likely effect?
o: Unemployment, as more labour is supplied than demanded
questions.why: At the higher wage, firms demand less labour while more people want to work, creating excess supply of labour.

questions.q: A worker on a means-tested benefit gets a pay rise, but loses benefit and pays more tax, so she is barely better off. What is this an example of?
questions.why: The withdrawal of benefits plus extra tax creates a very high effective marginal tax rate, reducing the incentive to earn more.

questions.q: The multiplier is larger when the marginal propensity to consume is…
questions.why: In a closed economy without government, k = 1/(1 − MPC).

questions.q: The natural rate of unemployment is associated with…
questions.why: It exists when the labour market is in equilibrium.

questions.q: Which best describes long-run economic growth?
o: A rise in AD in the short run
A rise in the price level
An increase in the productive capacity of the economy (LRAS shifts right)
questions.why: Examiners (2023): answers stressed short-run growth from AD rather than potential growth from rising LRAS.

questions.q: The marginal propensities to save, to tax and to import are 0.1, 0.2 and 0.2. Investment rises by $5 billion. By how much does national income change?
questions.why: MPW = 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.2 = 0.5, so the multiplier is 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2 and income rises by 2 × 5 = $10 billion.

questions.q: According to the quantity theory of money (MV = PT), if V and T are constant and the money supply rises by 8%, what happens to the price level?
questions.why: With V and T fixed, P changes in proportion to M, so an 8% rise in the money supply raises prices by 8%.

long.q: Explain how the multiplier works when government spending rises by $10 billion and the marginal propensity to withdraw is 0.25.
scheme: B1: multiplier = 1/MPW = 4
B1: national income rises by $40 billion
B1: each round of spending becomes someone's income, part of which is spent again
B1: withdrawals (saving, tax, imports) stop it rising for ever

questions.q: Quantitative easing means the central bank…
o: buys financial assets to increase the money supply
questions.why: It aims to lower long-term interest rates and boost spending.

questions.q: What does the Phillips curve show in the short run?
o: A direct link between GDP and exports
An inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation
A rise in both unemployment and inflation always
questions.why: In the long run it may be vertical at the natural rate.

questions.q: Which policy is supply-side?
o: Spending on training to raise labour productivity
questions.why: Supply-side policies aim to shift LRAS to the right.

questions.q: Which is an example of an automatic stabiliser?
o: A government announcing a new road-building programme
The central bank cutting its interest rate
A one-off cut in the rate of income tax
Tax revenue rising and benefit spending falling as incomes rise in a boom
questions.why: Automatic stabilisers change without any new decision, dampening the economic cycle; the other options are discretionary policy.

questions.q: According to the long-run (expectations-augmented) Phillips curve, what is the long-run effect of expansionary demand policy?
o: A permanent fall in unemployment with no extra inflation
Higher inflation with unemployment returning to its natural rate
questions.why: Once workers' inflation expectations adjust, unemployment returns to the natural rate, leaving only higher inflation; the long-run Phillips curve is vertical.

long.q: Assess whether supply-side policies are better than demand-side policies at reducing unemployment.
scheme: B1: supply-side: training, labour-market flexibility reduce structural unemployment
B1: but they take time and may be costly
B1: demand-side: fiscal or monetary expansion reduces cyclical unemployment quickly
B1: but risk inflation and do not fix structural problems
B1: a judgement depending on the cause of unemployment

questions.q: Which measure of development adjusts income for differences in prices between countries?
questions.why: PPP compares how much a unit of income buys in each country.

questions.q: What does the Marshall–Lerner condition state?
o: Depreciation improves the current account if the sum of export and import demand elasticities exceeds 1
questions.why: The J-curve shows it may worsen first.

questions.q: Which indicator measures development beyond income?
questions.why: HDI combines income, education and life expectancy.

questions.q: A country fixes its exchange rate against the US dollar. Market pressure starts to push its currency down. To keep the peg, the central bank is most likely to…
o: sell its own currency in exchange for foreign currency
buy its own currency using its foreign currency reserves
questions.why: Buying its own currency raises demand for it and supports the fixed rate; selling it or cutting interest rates would push it down further.

questions.q: Which indicator measures how many people in a country are deprived in health, education and living standards at the same time?
questions.why: The MPI counts overlapping deprivations in health, education and living standards; the Gini coefficient measures income inequality only.

long.q: Explain the possible effects of a depreciation of a country's currency on its current account.
scheme: B1: exports become cheaper abroad, imports dearer at home
B1: export volumes rise, import volumes fall
B1: the current account improves if PED for exports and imports is elastic (Marshall–Lerner)
B1: J-curve: it may worsen first
